title: Switch expressions (pattern-matching switch that returns a value)
hook: A switch expression picks the first matching pattern and returns a value — perfect when auth token kind should map to a processing mode, not a pile of if statements.

blocks.text: A switch expression looks like value switch { pattern => result, ... }. Each arm pairs a pattern with an expression that becomes the result. Unlike a classic switch statement, there is no fall-through, every arm must produce a value, and the whole expression evaluates to that value. Patterns can be constants, types, properties, relational tests, and more.

entries.plainDefinition: A C# expression that matches an input against patterns and returns the result of the first matching arm.
The _ pattern matches anything not caught by earlier arms. It is how you handle "everything else" or satisfy exhaustiveness.
The compiler check that every possible input value is handled by at least one arm.
entries.example: Switching on a bool needs true, false, or _ — the compiler warns if a case is missing.

blocks.text: Switch expressions turn branching into data. Instead of mutating a variable in each if branch, you assign once from a expression that maps input to output. The compiler warns when arms overlap or when coverage is incomplete. That is especially valuable for auth schemes, status codes, and enum handling where a silent default can become a security bug.

blocks.title: Expression vs statement
blocks.body: Use a switch expression when you need a value. Use a switch statement when arms must run multiple statements, call void methods, or break early. Do not stuff side effects into a switch expression just to avoid a statement.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Evaluate the input once
items.body: The value after switch is computed once, then tested against arms top to bottom.

items.title: Test each arm's pattern
items.body: The first pattern that matches wins. Later arms are never considered for that input.

items.title: Run the arm expression
items.body: The right-hand side of => is evaluated and becomes the result of the whole switch expression.

items.title: Compiler checks coverage
items.body: If no arm matches at run time, SwitchExpressionException is thrown. The compiler warns when arms are unreachable or coverage looks incomplete.

snippet.explanation: Each string constant is a pattern. The method returns AuthMode directly — no temp variable. The discard throws on unknown schemes instead of defaulting to a privileged mode.

snippet.label: Relational arms on a score
snippet.explanation: Arms are ordered. After < 50 matches, only values 50–99 remain for < 70. The or combinator rejects impossible percents before banding runs.

snippet.label: Pattern case in a switch statement (when you need statements)
snippet.explanation: When arms need void calls and multiple steps, use a switch statement. when is a guard evaluated after the pattern matches. Property patterns avoid nested ifs on Scheme and Version.

blocks.text: JavaScript switch statements fall through unless you break — a classic source of bugs. C# switch statements do not fall through (except empty cases stacked together). C# switch expressions never fall through at all; each arm is independent. TypeScript can approximate exhaustiveness with discriminated unions and a never check in default, but the compiler does not enforce it as strictly as C# does on closed types.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using _ => 0 as a silent default for token time-to-live or role assignment. Overlapping relational arms in the wrong order so a later arm never runs. Expecting fall-through like C or older JavaScript switch. Assuming enums are closed at run time — an enum can hold any int, so keep a discard arm.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: exhaustiveness is a compile-time contract — when you add a new enum member or auth scheme record, a missing switch arm becomes CS8509 or a nullable analysis warning. For enums cast from wire values, the compiler cannot prove closure — keep _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(token), token, null). Roslyn unreachable-arm diagnostics (CS8510) catch overlapping relational patterns before code review. In integration tests, feed every known token shape and one garbage int to prove the discard arm throws instead of defaulting to admin.

snippet.label: Exhaustiveness on closed records versus open enums
snippet.explanation: Line 5: compiler proves exhaustiveness on AuthScheme. Line 12: int from JSON can be any value — _ arm is mandatory; silent default would be a security bug.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: List every member; no discard needed

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying C# enums are always exhaustively checked at runtime — any int can be cast to an enum. Using _ => 0 or _ => Guest for auth decisions. Not knowing first-match-wins means arm order is semantic. Expecting fall-through like JavaScript switch without break.

interviewTakeaways: Switch expressions return a value; the compiler checks exhaustiveness on closed types and warns on unreachable arms.
Enums from wire data are not closed — always keep _ => throw; never silent default for auth or TTL.
In production, add a new enum member and let CS8509 force you to update every switch before merge.
60s: Switch expression returns a value. First match wins. Compiler exhaustiveness on closed enums. Open wire values need discard throw. TypeScript never helper is the analogue.
Follow-up: what diagnostic do you get when an arm is subsumed by an earlier pattern?
commonPitfalls: Saying enums are closed at runtime gets you rejected — any int casts to enum; discard throw is mandatory on wire data.
Using _ => 0 as a silent default for token TTL or role assignment.
Strong answer: 'Closed enum — compiler enforces arms. Wire int — _ throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Auth never gets a privileged discard default.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript switch falls through without break. C# switch statements do not (except empty cases). C# switch expressions cannot fall through at all. JavaScript has no exhaustiveness checker unless you use a never helper in TypeScript.
TypeScript switch on a union tag plus never in default is the analogue of C# exhaustive switch expressions on records or enums.
